segments.english: Akavya son of Mahalalel says: Consider three things and you will not come to the point of transgression. Know where you came from, and where you are going, and before whom you are destined to give account and reckoning. Where you came from: from a putrid drop. And where you are going: to a place of dust, maggot and worm. And before whom you are destined to give account and reckoning: before the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.

from a putrid drop

grammar: The saying has the form of a question and an answer: one imperative, דַּע 'know', governs three questions, and each is then answered in turn.
אִי אַתָּה בָא is the Mishnaic negative with a participle (a future: 'you will not come'); אִי stands for אֵין.
עָתִיד is an adjective (the pattern qatil), 'ready, destined', and takes the infinitive לִתֵּן: 'you are destined to give'.
מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים is a double superlative ('King of the kings of kings'): the construct chain piles up the title.
מֵאַיִן, וּלְאָן and וְלִפְנֵי מִי are three interrogative phrases, each repeated in the answer; the third answer reuses the whole question.
segments.note: דִּין וְחֶשְׁבּוֹן is rendered 'account and reckoning' (literally 'judgment and account'): the pair is a fixed idiom for a full accounting, and Bartenura reads the third item as the judgment before the King. Bartenura (3:1:1) reads the three items as three remedies: the putrid drop against pride, dust and worm against desire for wealth, the account against sin. The adjective סְרוּחָה is 'putrid'; Bartenura explains that the drop is called putrid because it is about to spoil once outside the womb.

commentary.summary: Bartenura says the drop is 'putrid' because it is about to rot once outside the womb, and that the one who looks at his origin is saved from pride, the one who looks at the place of dust, maggot and worm is saved from desire for wealth, and the one who looks at the coming account is saved from sin. The English follows his sense of the three items.

apparatus: Vilna reads עבירה for עֲבֵרָה, and ליתן for לִתֵּן (twice): spellings only.

Rabbeinu Yonah on 3:1 links the first consideration (whence you came) to lowliness of spirit, which saves from pride (Proverbs 16:5, cited there as 16:4), the second (dust and worm) to contempt for pleasures and wealth, as in Ecclesiastes, and the third to the shame of the soul before the King of kings.

segments.english: Rabbi Hanina, the deputy of the priests, says: Pray for the welfare of the government, for were it not for the fear of it, each man would have swallowed his fellow alive. Rabbi Hanina son of Teradion says: Two who sit with no words of Torah between them, this is a seat of scoffers, as it is said (Psalm 1): "and in the seat of scoffers he has not sat." But two who sit with words of Torah between them, the Shekhinah dwells among them, as it is said (Malachi 3): "Then those who fear the LORD spoke, each man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the LORD and for those who esteem his name." I know this only of two. From where do we learn that even for one who sits and occupies himself with Torah, the Holy One, blessed be He, sets a reward for him? As it is said (Lamentations 3): "He sits alone and murmurs, for he has taken it upon himself."

phrases.literal: 'he-sits alone and-is-still for he-took upon-him'; Bartenura and Rambam read וְיִדֹּם as the still, low voice of one who studies alone

grammar: The verse has three sayings: Rabbi Hanina the deputy on prayer for the government, Rabbi Hanina son of Teradion on Torah study in company, and its extension to one who studies alone.
שֶׁאִלְמָלֵא introduces a contrafactual clause; the apodosis is the perfect בְּלָעוֹ (בָּלַע with the suffix -וֹ, resuming רֵעֵהוּ): 'would have swallowed him'.
שְׁנַיִם שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִין וְאֵין בֵּינֵיהֶן ... is a casus pendens: 'Two who sit and there is not between them ... this is ...'; הֲרֵי זֶה opens the main clause.
וְיֵשׁ and וְאֵין are the existential particles ('there is' and 'there is not') followed by a subject in the construct: 'words of Torah'.
מִנַּיִן is the standard Talmudic question, 'from where (do we learn)'; the answers are verses, quoted by their source.
segments.note: סְגַן הַכֹּהֲנִים is 'the deputy of the priests'; the English keeps the title. מַלְכוּת is 'the government' (the sages read the ruling power, including foreign rule: Bartenura 3:2:1). The sentence 'each man would have swallowed his fellow alive' (Bartenura 3:2:2 cites Habakkuk 1:14, 'like the fish of the sea') is a contrafactual. The last verse, נָטַל עָלָיו, is read in the Mishnah as 'he has taken it upon himself': Bartenura 3:2:5 reads 'as though the whole giving of the Torah were for him alone'; וְיִדֹּם is rendered 'murmurs': Bartenura (3:2:4) and Rambam (3:2:2) read it as the soft voice of one who studies in a whisper; Rabbeinu Yonah reads silent study in thought. In Lamentations 3:28 the verse is more likely 'Let him sit alone and be silent, for he has laid it upon him' (God has laid it on him).

commentary.summary: Bartenura says the 'government' here includes even the governments of the nations of the world; the English follows with the general word 'the government'.

Bartenura cites Habakkuk 1:14 ('and you make man like the fish of the sea'): as among fish the greater swallows the lesser, so would men without the fear of government (Avodah Zarah 4a). The English follows this reading of 'swallow'.
Bartenura says, 'Behold here are two': the verse, 'each man to his fellow', shows two speakers. The English follows this proof.
Bartenura: וְיִדֹּם is 'a term of a still, thin voice' (קוֹל דְּמָמָה דַּקָּה), the way one who studies alone studies in a whisper. The English follows with 'murmurs'.
Bartenura reads כִּי נָטַל עָלָיו as 'as if the giving of the whole Torah had been for him alone'; the English follows with 'he has taken it upon himself'.

Rambam (anchored here by the pack, but commenting on 3:1) says that looking at whence one came brings humility, looking at one's end brings contempt for worldly affairs, and looking to the greatness of the One who commands (הַמְצַוֶּה) brings haste to obey His commandments; one who holds these three will not sin at all. This bears on 3:1, not on the plain sense of 3:2.

Rambam says that 'seat of scoffers' means any seat in which words of Torah are not spoken, as the end of Psalm 1:1-2 shows: because his delight was in the Torah of the LORD he did not sit in a seat of scoffers where there is no Torah. The English follows this reading.

Rambam quotes the Talmud (Berakhot 6a): one who sits and studies has the Shekhinah with him (Exodus 20:21); two have their words written in the Book of Remembrance; and he explains וְיִדֹּם as 'quiet speech, the soft voice' (Aramaic שתיק), and כִּי נָטַל עָלָיו as 'as if the giving of the whole Torah had been for him alone'. The English follows him.

Rabbeinu Yonah: the one who is silent and meditates in Torah is as if he took upon himself the yoke of Torah in thought; he cites the Rama's reading, that one who studies alone is as if he fulfilled the whole Torah, with וְיִדֹּם as speech.

apparatus: Psalm 1:1 (the last clause, וּבְמוֹשַׁב לֵצִים לֹא יָשָׁב).
Malachi 3:16 (אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי יְיָ ...): the Mishnah quotes the verse to its end; the proof is in אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ, two speakers.
Lamentations 3:28 (יֵשֵׁב בָּדָד וְיִדֹּם כִּי נָטַל עָלָיו).
Vilna reads ה for יְיָ (three times), ולחושבי for וּלְחֹשְׁבֵי, שאפילו for שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ, וידום for וְיִדֹּם; Vilna omits שְׁרוּיָה ('dwells') at 3:2.48.
3:2.34 תהלים, 3:2.51 מלאכי and 3:2.88 איכה are the source names of the quoted verses; 3:2.35, 3:2.52 and 3:2.89 are letter numerals for the chapters.
Vilna adds the verse number after each source: (תהלים א) א, (מלאכי ג) טז, (איכה ג) כח.

segments.english: Rabbi Shimon says: Three who ate at one table and did not say words of Torah over it, it is as if they ate of sacrifices to the dead, as it is said (Isaiah 28): "For all the tables are full of vomit and filth, with no place." But three who ate at one table and said words of Torah over it, it is as if they ate from the table of the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said (Ezekiel 41): "And he spoke to me: This is the table that is before the LORD."

tokens.note: כְּאִלּוּ "as if", a conditional of comparison.
letter numeral, chapter 28 (the pack's lexicon link to כֹּחַ does not fit).
צֹאָה "excrement, filth".
בְּלִי "without".
מָקוֹם "place", and also the Mishnaic name of God, "the Place" (see Bartenura on בְּלִי מָקוֹם).
the genitive particle שֶׁל, here with the pronominal suffix on שֻׁלְחָן: "the table of".
מָקוֹם without article is the name of God, "the Omnipresent" (literally "the Place").
letter numeral, chapter 41.
Piel wayyiqtol of דבר: 'and he spoke'. The pack links it to the noun דָּבָר, so no sense is given.

grammar: The saying sets two sentences in opposition: three who ate and did not speak words of Torah, and three who ate and did (אֲבָל, 'but'); both have the form 'three who ... as if they ate ...'.
שֶׁאָכְלוּ is a relative clause with a perfect: 'who ate'; the sentence is a casus pendens with כְּאִלּוּ opening the main clause.
מִשֻּׁלְחָנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם uses the Mishnaic double genitive: 'from his table, of the Place'.
מָקוֹם is a name of God, 'the Place' (the Omnipresent), here without the article; בְּלִי מָקוֹם in Isaiah can be read 'with no place', and the sages read it as 'without the Place'.
The two scripture proofs are quoted with their sources (Isaiah 28:8, Ezekiel 41:22), the second ending with 'the table that is before the LORD'.
segments.note: מָקוֹם בָּרוּךְ הוּא is translated 'the Omnipresent, blessed be He' by the project's decision; the literal sense of מָקוֹם is 'the Place'. מִזִּבְחֵי מֵתִים is 'sacrifices to the dead', the sacrifices of idols (Bartenura and Rambam; Psalm 106:28). In Isaiah 28:8 בְּלִי מָקוֹם means 'with no room'; Bartenura reads it as 'without the Place', for they did not mention the name of the Place at the table, so the English 'with no place' keeps both readings.

commentary.summary: Bartenura adds a legal note, 'I heard': saying the grace after meals at the table counts as saying words of Torah over it. The English keeps 'words of Torah' and records his sense.
Bartenura says 'sacrifices to the dead' are offerings to idols, as in Psalm 106:28 ('and they were joined to Baal-peor and ate sacrifices to the dead'). The English follows.
Bartenura says idolatry is called צֹאָה 'filth', as in Isaiah 30:22: 'You shall say to it, Get out (צֵא)'. The English keeps 'filth' and follows.
Bartenura reads בְּלִי מָקוֹם as 'because they did not mention the name of the Place, blessed be He, at the table'. The English 'with no place' keeps the plain sense and records this reading here.

Bartenura: as soon as one speaks words of Torah, the table is called 'the table that is before the LORD'. Some say the proof is from the head of the verse, 'the altar of wood, three cubits (אַמּוֹת)': read not אַמּוֹת but אִמּוֹת, 'mothers' (sources), three, for Torah, Prophets and Writings (or Scripture, Mishnah and Talmud), which a man must speak of at the table; so Rashi explained. The English follows the first reading.
Rambam says 'sacrifices to the dead' is the offering of idol worship, as Scripture calls it, and Isaiah calls it 'vomit and filth' to scorn it. The English follows.

apparatus: Isaiah 28:8 (כִּי כָּל שֻׁלְחָנוֹת מָלְאוּ קִיא צֹאָה בְּלִי מָקוֹם).
Ezekiel 41:22 (the last words: זֶה הַשֻּׁלְחָן אֲשֶׁר לִפְנֵי יְיָ); the Mishnah's text of Ezekiel runs וַיְדַבֵּר אֵלַי.
Vilna reads כאילו for כְּאִלּוּ (twice) and צואה for צֹאָה.
3:3.19 ישעיה and 3:3.47 יחזקאל are the source names; 3:3.20 כח and 3:3.48 מא are letter numerals (28 and 41), and the pack's lemma links for them (כֹּחַ, מָא) are not the sense here.
Vilna adds the verse number after each source: (ישעיה כח) ח, (יחזקאל מא) כב.

segments.english: Rabbi Hanina son of Hakhinai says: One who is awake at night, or who walks on the road alone, and who turns his heart to idleness: this one is answerable with his life.

tokens.note: Nifal participle of עור "to wake, rouse oneself" with the article: "the one who wakes".
Piel participle of הלך: "who goes about".
יְחִידִי, the Mishnaic adverbial form of יָחִיד: 'alone, by himself'.
Piel participle of פנה 'to clear, make room': he empties his heart for idle things.
בַּטָּלָה "idleness, vain things".
Hitpael participle of חיב "to be liable, to incur guilt".
נֶפֶשׁ "soul, life".

phrases.english: Rabbi Hanina son of Hakhinai says
One who is awake at night
or who walks on the road alone
phrases.literal: 'and-the-one-walking on-the-road alone'; the second situation, alternative to the first

phrases.english: and who turns his heart to idleness
phrases.literal: 'and-the-one-clearing his-heart to-idleness'; Bartenura reads this clause as the condition of both situations

phrases.english: this one is answerable with his life

grammar: Three participles with the article (הַנֵּעוֹר, הַמְהַלֵּךְ, הַמְפַנֶּה) head the sentence; Bartenura reads the third as the condition of the first two: one who is awake at night or walks alone, and turns his heart to idle things.
הֲרֵי זֶה opens the main clause ('this one ...'), resuming the subject.
הַנֵּעוֹר is a Nifal participle of עור, 'is awake'; מְהַלֵּךְ and מְפַנֶּה are Piel participles. The Piel of פנה is 'to clear, make room': he frees his heart for idleness.
מִתְחַיֵּב is a Hitpael participle: 'makes himself liable'. The Vilna spelling is מתחייב.
בְּנַפְשׁוֹ 'with his life': he puts his own life at risk (Bartenura: demons by night, robbers on the road).
יְחִידִי, 'alone, by himself', is the Mishnaic adverbial form of יָחִיד.
segments.note: מִתְחַיֵּב בְּנַפְשׁוֹ is rendered 'is answerable with his life'. The English follows Bartenura: the night (3:4:1-2) is the time of demons and the lone traveller is in danger from robbers and other harm, and the one in either case who turns his heart to idle thoughts is guilty, for words of Torah would have guarded him. Read grammatically as three separate subjects, each participle with its own article, the saying would make the waking and the journey liable by themselves; the commentators do not read it so.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: the one awake at night and the one walking alone on the road are guilty when he thinks idle things in his heart (וּמְחַשֵּׁב בְּלִבּוֹ דִּבְרֵי הֲבַאי): the third clause is the condition of the first two. The English follows.

Bartenura: night is the time of demons, and one who walks alone on the road is in danger from robbers and many evils; had he thought of words of Torah, it would have guarded him. Hence he is liable with his life only when his heart is turned to idleness. The English follows.

apparatus: Vilna reads מתחייב for מִתְחַיֵּב: spelling only.

segments.english: Rabbi Nehunya son of Hakanah says: Whoever takes upon himself the yoke of Torah, they remove from him the yoke of the government and the yoke of worldly occupation. And whoever throws off from himself the yoke of Torah, they place upon him the yoke of the government and the yoke of worldly occupation.

grammar: The saying is two parallel conditional sentences: כָּל + participle, then a plural participle (מַעֲבִירִין, נוֹתְנִין) as an impersonal passive.
The two sentences are antithetic and in the same order: the one who takes the yoke of Torah has the other yokes removed (מַעֲבִירִין), the one who throws it off has them placed on him (נוֹתְנִין).
הַמְקַבֵּל and הַפּוֹרֵק are articular participles used as the subject after כָּל, 'whoever takes / whoever throws off'; קִבֵּל עָלָיו and פָּרַק מִמֶּנּוּ are the opposite idioms for a yoke.
עֹל תּוֹרָה is a construct chain 'the yoke of Torah'; the same pattern, עֹל מַלְכוּת, עֹל דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, follows.
דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ ('the way of the land') is an idiom for the ordinary business of life, and in Avot often for the worldly occupation of earning a living.
segments.note: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ is rendered 'worldly occupation' by the project's decision, following Bartenura (3:5:2: the toil and labour of earning a living); Rambam (3:5:3) reads 'the toil of the times'. מַלְכוּת is 'the government': Bartenura says the burden of the king and officials, Rambam the toil of the king and his armies. The Vilna spelling is עול for עֹל. The pack's lemma link for עֹל (עַל) is a different word; the sense is 'yoke'.

commentary.summary: Bartenura glosses עֹל מַלְכוּת as the burden of the king and the officers. The English follows with 'the yoke of the government'.
Bartenura glosses דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ as the toil and labour of earning a living, since the work of the one who studies is blessed. The English follows with 'worldly occupation'.
Bartenura says 'throws off the yoke of Torah' means one who says, 'The yoke of Torah is hard and I cannot bear it'. The English follows with 'throws off'.
Rambam glosses עֹל תּוֹרָה as persistence in reading (הַתְמָדַת הַקְּרִיאָה). The English keeps 'the yoke of Torah' and follows him.
Rambam glosses עֹל מַלְכוּת as the toil of the king and his troops. The English follows with 'the yoke of the government'.

Rambam glosses עֹל דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ as 'the toil of the time (zeman)': in reward for taking the yoke of Torah, God spares him the toil of the age. The English follows Bartenura's 'worldly occupation' instead and records this.

apparatus: Vilna reads עול for עֹל (four times) and ועול for וְעֹל (twice): spelling only.

segments.english: Rabbi Halafta son of Dosa, of Kefar Hananiah, says: Ten who sit and occupy themselves with Torah, the Shekhinah dwells among them, as it is said (Psalm 82): "God stands in the congregation of God." And from where even five? As it is said (Amos 9): "and his bundle upon the earth he has founded." And from where even three? As it is said (Psalm 82): "In the midst of judges he judges." And from where even two? As it is said (Malachi 3): "Then those who fear the LORD spoke, each man to his fellow, and the LORD listened and heard, and so on." And from where even one? As it is said (Exodus 20): "In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you."

grammar: The verse is a descending ladder: ten, five, three, two, one, each given a scripture proof introduced by וּמִנַּיִן אֲפִלּוּ 'and from where even'.
The first sentence has the same casus pendens as 3:2: 'Ten who sit ... the Shekhinah dwells among them'.
שְׁכִינָה שְׁרוּיָה בֵּינֵיהֶם: a feminine noun with a passive participle of שרה, 'dwelling', with the suffix בֵּינֵיהֶם 'among them'.
The proof texts are cut off at the point of the proof: the quotation from Malachi ends with וְגוֹ' ('and so on'), and Exodus 20:21 is quoted from בְּכָל הַמָּקוֹם.

אֲגֻדָּה ('bundle') is read as a hand with five fingers (Rambam, Rabbeinu Yonah) or as a bundle of three elements or three stalks of hyssop (Bartenura); the verse is a wordplay on the number in the proof.
segments.note: The proof of the five rests on אֲגֻדָּתוֹ, 'his bundle': Rambam and Rabbeinu Yonah read a bundle as what one binds in one hand, which has five fingers. Bartenura's own text reverses the two middle proofs: five from 'in the midst of judges he judges' (three judges and two litigants) and three from 'his bundle' (fire, air and water around the earth, or three stalks of hyssop); he gives the order of this text as the reading of 'some books', with the hand of five fingers. The English keeps 'his bundle'. In the first proof the congregation (עֵדָה) is not fewer than ten (Rambam; Bartenura from the spies, Numbers 14:27). In the third, אֱלֹהִים is 'judges' (a court of three: Rambam, Bartenura), and the English follows them. 'Kefar Hananiah' is a place, as in the pack. The pack's lemma link for אֵל (the particle אַל) does not fit; the word is אֵל 'God', in 'the congregation of God'.

commentary.summary: Bartenura says 'we read: ten who sat in judgment' (עֲשָׂרָה שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים בַּדִּין). The English follows the printed text (Torah study) and records his reading.
Bartenura says a congregation (עֵדָה) is not fewer than ten, as in Numbers 14:27, where the ten spies minus Joshua and Caleb are 'this evil congregation'. The English follows.

Bartenura (his heading reads 'and from where even five' with this verse): 'in the midst of judges he judges' gives three judges and two litigants, five. The English follows the base text, which proves three from this verse, as Bartenura himself explains in the reading of 'some books' (3:6:4); his own order is recorded here.

Bartenura's text reads 'even three' with 'his bundle': fire, air and water, three, surround the foundation of the earth; or a bundle of hyssop of three stalks. He adds that some books read 'even five' with this verse, for a man binds with one hand of five fingers, and the whole of the fingers is called a bundle; the head of the verse, 'who builds His upper chambers in the heavens', means that the Shekhinah descends when a bundle studies Torah; and then 'even three' from 'in the midst of judges', for judges are three. The English follows the 'some books' reading, which is the base text.

Bartenura: נָטַל עָלָיו is a term of covering (לְשׁוֹן סְכָךְ), as the Targum renders וְסַכֹּתָ 'and you shall cover' by וְתַטֵּל: the Shekhinah covers him. The comment belongs to the verse of 3:2 (Lamentations 3:28), not to the plain sense of 3:6.

Rambam: a congregation (עֵדָה) is not fewer than ten, and a court not fewer than three, who are called אֱלֹהִים for judgment; an אֲגֻדָּה is what a man binds with one hand, which has five fingers, so the five fingers are called a bundle. The English follows all three points: 'congregation', 'judges' and 'his bundle'.

apparatus: Psalm 82:1 (אֱלֹהִים נִצָּב בַּעֲדַת אֵל).
Amos 9:6 (וַאֲגֻדָּתוֹ עַל אֶרֶץ יְסָדָהּ).
Psalm 82:1 (בְּקֶרֶב אֱלֹהִים יִשְׁפֹּט).
Malachi 3:16 (אָז נִדְבְּרוּ יִרְאֵי יְיָ אִישׁ אֶל רֵעֵהוּ וַיַּקְשֵׁב יְיָ וַיִּשְׁמָע ...).
Exodus 20:21 (בְּכָל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר אַזְכִּיר אֶת שְׁמִי אָבֹא אֵלֶיךָ וּבֵרַכְתִּיךָ).
Vilna omits בֶן דּוֹסָא (3:6.3-4) and תהלים פב (3:6.37-38); reads אפילו for אֲפִלּוּ, ואגודתו for וַאֲגֻדָּתוֹ, ישפוט for יִשְׁפֹּט and וגומר for וְגוֹ'.
Vilna adds the verse number after the sources: (תהלים פב) א, (עמוס ט) ו, (מלאכי ג) טז, (שמות כ) כ.
Bartenura (3:6:1) reads עֲשָׂרָה שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים בַּדִּין 'ten who were sitting in judgment' (גָּרְסִינַן), and in 3:6:3-4 his text proves five from Psalm 82:1 and three from Amos 9:6.
